Skin graft viability

One small split-wound trial found fewer graft dehiscences with PBM, and an uncontrolled burn case series reported complete healing in 13 patients. Rat experiments often found improved integration, but results differed by wavelength.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small split-wound trial found fewer graft dehiscences with PBM, and an uncontrolled burn case series reported complete healing in 13 patients. Rat experiments often found improved integration, but results differed by wavelength.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven relevant publications comprise five rat experiments on full-thickness skin-graft integration and two human burn-wound reports mapped from the broader burns category. The human evidence includes one self-controlled randomized study of nine patients and one uncontrolled 13-case series. Donor-site healing and studies using PBM instead of grafting were excluded. No duplicate reports were identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In the nine-person study, each patient had treated and comparison areas after graft surgery. The PBM-treated areas had fewer wound dehiscences than those receiving standard dressings, with a statistically significant difference reported by the authors. This is a direct clinical result for graft-site separation, but the small sample limits precision (Kazemikhoo et al. 2018).

A separate case series described 13 people with severe diabetic burn wounds who received split-thickness grafting together with PBM. All were reported to have healed by eight weeks, including patients considered candidates for amputation. Because the series had no comparison group and combined light with graft surgery and routine care, it cannot show how much PBM contributed (Dahmardehei et al. 2016).

Animal evidence

The five rat experiments mostly reported better graft adhesion, healing, inflammation, or tissue integration with PBM. One study found increased mast cells, blood vessels, collagen, and FGF expression after 660-nm treatment, without a difference in IL-4. Another reported improved healing and modulation of local inflammation at 6 or 10 J/cm² applied every five days. In nicotine-exposed rats, both 660-nm red and 830-nm near-infrared light facilitated graft integration. A 2024 comparison was less uniformly favorable: 660-nm red light had the lowest necrosis at day seven, whereas 808-nm near-infrared treatment showed increasing necrosis over time and performed worse than control on integration measures (Castro et al. 2019; Moreira et al. 2020; Espósito et al. 2024).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human split-wound trial applied 655-nm red visible light to the graft bed at 2 J/cm² and 808-nm near-infrared light to the margins at 6 J/cm² over seven days. The case series used 650-nm red and 810-nm near-infrared light at the wound, along with intravenous 660-nm red light, for a total of about 10 to 15 sessions. Rat studies used red 660- or 630-nm light and near-infrared 808-, 830-, or 850-nm light. Fluence, application points, and timing differed, and the animal wavelength comparison argues against assuming all protocols perform alike.

Interpretation

The small controlled human study found fewer dehiscences, while the uncontrolled series reported complete healing after combined grafting and PBM. Rat studies often found improved integration, but wavelength-related results were mixed. The evidence supports a clinical result worth testing further and a broader favorable animal pattern, without establishing a reliable human graft-survival protocol.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for clinical reduction in graft dehiscence.

Low to moderate for graft integration in rat models.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The nine-person split-wound trial found fewer dehiscences, but the clinical sample is very small, and the 13-case series had no control group. Five rat experiments report several favorable integration measures, although wavelength effects differed. Larger controlled burn or reconstructive cohorts with blinded graft-take assessment and follow-up would be needed to support a firmer clinical rating.
